title: Scam Awareness 101 & Basic Review
objectives: The four on-chain checks that catch most new-token scams
How to read a mint's authorities yourself, and what a snapshot can't promise
The whole basic layer, seen as one picture before Tier 2

steps.title: The dark side of permissionless
steps.body:
Anything you can build on Solana in thirty seconds, a scammer can build too. The weapon isn't a server hack or a stolen password - it's a new wallet's habit of not reading, and a token that's been quietly left able to do something ugly.

The good news is that everything a token can do to you is written in public account data. Freeze a balance, print new supply, pull the pool - each one is a switch, and switches are either on or off where anyone can look.

That's the mindset this lesson is really about. Stop asking "is this a good investment?" and start asking "what is this token allowed to do to me?". The second question has a factual answer, on-chain, right now, and it's the one that keeps you out of the traps.

steps.title: The four checks that matter
steps.body:
Before buying any brand-new token, four checks take about two minutes and catch most of what's waiting for you.

**1. Freeze authority.** If it's still active, the creator can freeze your token account, which means you can hold the token but never sell or move it. The only safe state is revoked.

**2. Mint authority.** If it's still active, the creator can print unlimited supply and sell it. This is the plainest <Term id="rug_pull">rug pull</Term> there is, and the only safe state is revoked.

**3. Who holds the pool.** Whoever holds the <Term id="lp_token">LP tokens</Term> controls the liquidity. If the creator still holds them, they can pull the entire pool in one transaction and leave you with a token nobody can buy. Look for a burn or a lock - and if it's a lock, check the date, not just the fact of it.

**4. Holder concentration.** If a handful of non-pool wallets hold most of the supply, the price is really a countdown to whenever they decide to sell. Concentration isn't proof of a scam, but it does mean a few people can end the token whenever they choose.

No single flag here is conclusive. Together they're a filter - and a launch that fails two of them is one you didn't need to buy.

steps.title: Checking authorities yourself
steps.body:
None of this needs a special tool. A block explorer shows a mint's authorities in plain text, and the Token program exposes them on the command line:

`spl-token authorize <MINT_ADDRESS> mint --disable`

`spl-token authorize <MINT_ADDRESS> freeze --disable`

Those two commands are what "revoked" means underneath. Run them and the authority fields become `None`, permanently.

The catch is that a check is only as good as the address you checked. Revoked can't be un-revoked, but a scam can also ship a second mint with the same name and ticker to catch people who verify the wrong thing. Copy the mint address from a source you trust and check that - never the name.

questions.prompt: You inspect a new token and see 'Freeze Authority: Active'. What does that mean for you?
options: The creator can block your account from selling or transferring the token
The fee is fixed at 0.000005 SOL
questions.explainRight: It can freeze your account, so you could hold the token and never be able to sell it.
questions.explainWrong: An active freeze authority lets the creator block your account from selling or transferring.

questions.prompt: What actually proves a creator cannot mint infinite new tokens?
options: A verification badge on a social profile
Permanently revoking the mint authority on-chain, so it reads None
questions.explainRight: Revoking on-chain is the only proof. A badge on a profile proves nothing about the mint.
questions.explainWrong: Only revoking the mint authority guarantees the supply can't grow.

steps.title: The whole basic layer, in one pass
steps.body:
You've covered all of Tier 1. Worth a minute to see it as one picture.

A <Term id="wallet">wallet</Term> has an <Term id="address">address</Term> you share and a key you never do, and a <Term id="signature">signature</Term> is you approving one specific action and nothing else. Fees are 5,000 lamports per signature; <Term id="rent">rent</Term> is a refundable deposit you get back when you close an account. Tokens live in their own accounts - the <Term id="mint">mint</Term> defines the asset, your account holds your slice - and every balance is an integer scaled by <Term id="decimals">decimals</Term>.

Markets are pools running constant-product maths, so your own order moves the price and <Term id="slippage">slippage</Term> is the floor you refuse to fill below. Two tokens with the same price can be completely different sizes once you multiply by supply, and <Term id="fdv">FDV</Term> is the whole thing including what's still locked. <Term id="tvl">TVL</Term> is a deposit figure the protocol partly controls, so treat it as a signal, not a fact.

And the four checks from this lesson are the practical version of all of it: mint authority, freeze authority, who holds the pool, and who holds the supply.

Tier 2 starts where the money actually moves - liquidity, lending, and the ways those two break.
